meta.title: Espresso Is Older Than Its Crema | How the espresso machine was invented, 1884 to 1961
meta.family_reason: It follows one object, the espresso machine, in strict time order from its first patent (1884) to the standard it works at today. At 150 seconds the belief-reversal families (A1, A3: 4 to 6 minutes, withheld subject) do not fit; C covers 1 to 6 minutes and opens with the result.
meta.lead: The machine is older than the crema by more than fifty years
meta.logline: The espresso machine was patented to make coffee instantly; the crema we now read as the mark of espresso arrived more than fifty years later, when a piston replaced steam, and it was first sold under a name other than espresso.
meta.audience_belief: Espresso, crema and all, is an old Italian tradition that has always been made this way.
meta.axis_fact: The pressure gauge: the first machines pushed water at about 1.5 bar and never passed 2, so they made no crema. Crema appears only after Achille Gaggia's piston (patent of Sept. 5, 1938; lever patent 1947), more than fifty years after the first patent of 1884, and it was sold as 'crema caffè' to set it apart from espresso. Today's standard is 9 bar.
meta.materials: Open-license live-action stock (Pexels, Pixabay, Mixkit, Coverr): espresso extraction, cups, hands, lever machine. Vector graphics: pressure gauge, piston cutaway, timeline, typography. Public-domain patent drawings: Moriondo 1884 (Wikimedia Commons), Bezzera U.S. Patent 726,793 (1903). No commissioned shooting, no generated images.

sources.label: Jimmy Stamp, 'The Long History of the Espresso Machine', Smithsonian Magazine, 2012
sources.checked: Moriondo granted a patent in 1884 for 'new steam machinery for the economic and instantaneous confection of coffee beverage'; boiler heated to 1.5 bar; 'purely a bulk brewer'. Early steam machines 'at best, two bars', 1.5 to 2 bar without burning the coffee; burnt or bitter taste. Gaggia a 'Milanese café owner'; lever raises pressure to 8 to 10 bar; crema comes with the lever machine. Faema E61 (1961): motorized pump, nine bar. Also says early machines made 'up to 1,000 cups of coffee per hour' (NOT used: S6 says 150) and that Pavoni bought the patents in 1903 (year not used: S6 gives a deed of 1 Sept. 1902).

sources.label: Jonathan Morris, 'Making Italian Espresso, Making Espresso Italian', Food and History 8(2), 2010, pp. 155-183 (author's pre-print, University of Hertfordshire)
sources.checked: pp. 8, 12-18 of the pre-print. The claim that espresso is an unchanging tradition 'does not stand up in historical terms'. Bezzera registered his patent in 1901; Pavoni's Ideale of 1905 was the first espresso machine in commercial production; both exhibited at the 1906 fair in Milan. Pre-war espresso was black, tasted bitter and burnt because of the steam, and 'lacked any of the mousse or crema topping' at around 1.5 bar. Gaggia, 'a Milanese bar owner', patented a rotating-handle piston in 1938, not manufactured; by 1941 Italy 'ceased to import coffee altogether'. 1947 lever patent with a spring: pressure 'from three to twelve atmospheres'; oils and colloids form the crema; the drink was renamed 'crema caffè' to distinguish it from espresso. Machine slogans 'Crema caffè naturale' and 'It works without steam'. 1961 Faema E61: electric pump, 'a relatively constant 9 bars'. INEI standard: 9 bar.

sources.label: Luigi Bezzera, 'Coffee-Making Machine', U.S. Patent 726,793, patented April 28, 1903 (filed June 10, 1902)
sources.checked: Patent number, dates, title; heading 'LUIGI BEZZERA, OF MILAN, ITALY, ASSIGNOR TO DESIDERIO PAVONI, OF MILAN, ITALY'; drawing sheet headers; the quoted sentence 'By means of my appliance, on the other hand, the quantity of coffee necessary for a single cup is prepared separately, so that fresh coffee is always served.' Read in the Google Patents text and in the patent PDF (patentimages.storage.googleapis.com/dd/70/81/35aa2b0604438b/US726793.pdf). U.S. patent text and drawings of 1903 are in the public domain.

sources.label: Gaggia Milano, 'Our History' (manufacturer's history page)
sources.checked: Patent no. 365726 filed Sept. 5, 1938 for 'Lampo': hot water pressure instead of steam, 'a soft layer of crema naturale'. Second patent (1947): lever and spring. 1948: first machine, Tipo Classica. Slogan on the machines: 'Crema caffè naturale - Funziona senza vapore'. DISAGREES with S2 on when crema first appears (1938 here, 1947 lever in S2): the script says 'more than fifty years', true for both (54 and 63).

sources.label: Gaggia Professional (Evoca Group), 'About Gaggia'
sources.checked: 1938 patent no. 365726 'for a steam-free coffee machine'; the 1947 lever reached '8-9 atmospheres'; machines bear the words 'Crema caffè naturale funziona senza vapore'. Lever pressure differs across S1 (8-10 bar), S2 (3-12 atm, rising and falling) and here (8-9 atm): no lever pressure figure is used on screen.

sources.label: Elena Locatelli, 'La Pavoni. Dal 1905 macchine per il caffè' (company monograph, 2005), pp. 5-19
sources.checked: Official gazette of 13 Jan. 1904: Bezzera's patent 'Innovation in equipment designed to instantly prepare and serve coffee as a drink' (certificate of 5 June 1902) transferred to Desiderio Pavoni by deed of 1 Sept. 1902. Bezzera's machine worked at 1.5 atm. Ideale, 1905. Sign at the 1906 Milan fair: 'Bezzera L. Caffè Espresso'. Says the machines made 'up to 150 cups of coffee per hour' (disagrees with S1's 1,000: no cups-per-hour figure is used). Gives 19 November 1901 for Bezzera's filing where other secondary sources give 19 December: only the year 1901 is used.

sources.label: Angelo Moriondo, patent drawing, Bollettino delle Privative Industriali, 1884 (Wikimedia Commons file page)
sources.checked: Image viewed: the sheet is headed 'Bollettino delle Privative Industriali - Anno 1884' and carries the printed title 'MORIONDO ANGELO. Nuovi apparecchi a vapore per la confezione economica ed istantanea del caffè in bevanda sistema A. Moriondo'. File description: patent vol. 33 no. 256, dated May 16, 1884. Marked public domain. The date May 16, 1884 rests on this file description and matching secondary pages; S1 confirms the year and the title.

sources.label: Bezzera, 'Company History' (manufacturer's page)
sources.checked: '1901 Luigi Bezzera patented espresso coffee machine'; first machine shown at the Milan International Fair in 1906. The page dates U.S. Patent 726,793 to 'May 28, 1902', which is the day Bezzera signed the specification; the patent record (S3) gives filing June 10, 1902 and grant April 28, 1903, and the script follows the record.

sources.label: Italian Espresso National Institute (INEI), 'The Certified Italian Espresso and Cappuccino' (brochure, 2006)
sources.checked: PDF opened (pp. 1-3 read: the Institute, founded 1998, certificate Csqa n. 214 of 24 Sept. 1999). The parameter table 'Entry water pressure 9 bar ± 1' was confirmed from the search excerpt of this PDF and from S2, which reports the same INEI figure.

review_notes: Manual check, scene and sentence: c23 'rose as foam' partly repeats what the glass shows; kept because the sentence's work is the cause (pressure, the coffee's own oils) and the foam is the grammatical end of that cause. c07 shows the Italian title while the sentence gives its English sense; kept as a translation of text in the picture.

Manual check, English periods: the card spec says editorial lines take no period, but the linter can only see a closed English card by its period. Closed cards therefore end with a period, open cards with a comma or nothing, noun-stop cards (c08, c10, c20, c27) carry end: '명사'.

Manual check, reading time: the production reading floor is not checked for English. Every text card was checked by hand against words/3 + 2 s (quote cards with attribution + 1.5 s); the shortest margin is c02 (7 words, 4.5 s against 4.3 s).

Editor pass after skill 0.6.0: footage cards retyped. Footage of espresso itself is 실사 even though it is sourced, not shot; only c17 (plain black coffee standing in for the pre-war drink) is 스톡. Search terms moved from note to visual.footage.

Editor pass: c10 and c11 lengthened to meet the English reading floor (words/3 + 2 s); the time came from c12, c27 and c29. c16 "three more decades" became "decades more" so the card carries one figure. c27 sets two figures side by side on purpose (compare: true).
Positions given in visual.desc for sourced footage ("cup in the lower third") are wishes, not conditions. Production crops, shifts and darkens the clip to clear the text zone (04, section 8).
c04 (name card) was kept as the film's title card although the object is familiar; the writer noted it reads as surplus. It gives the lead a beat to land before the patent sheet.

After production (2026-11-12, see examples/espresso/production-notes.md): c20 was produced as a diagram, not live action. No clip of a lever being pulled was found on Pexels, Pixabay or Mixkit, so the fallback now written on c20 was used.
After production: c30 (sources, 16 words in 5 s) is too short to read; the new source-card-time check flags it. It is left as produced. In a revision, give it 7.5 s or split it in two.

After production: the music could not start on the first frame. The chosen track is 131 s and the film 150 s, so the film opens on the sound of the machine alone and the music enters at 15.5 s; its ending lands on the last line.
assumptions: Length: 150 seconds, taken from the brief ('about 150 seconds').
Audience belief: the brief's suggestion was kept after research; Morris (S2) describes exactly this belief and says it does not stand up historically.

Language of the file: on-screen text (lines, label, attribution) is English. Scene descriptions, carries, motion, notes and the design fields in meta are also written in English so that an English-language production and stock search can use them; fields whose values the skill defines as fixed Korean terms (kind, visual.type, hook_mode, ending.type, callback_kind, frame, quote_form, status, pos) keep the Korean values. Beat names keep the Korean names of the C beat sheet with an English gloss.
Open-license live-action stock is typed as visual.type '스톡'; public-domain patent drawings as '기록'; vector graphics as '도해' or '타이포'.

English reading time: the production floor in the card spec is defined for Korean only (characters/7 + 2 s). For English this script uses words/3 + 2 s as its own floor, plus 1.5 s on the card that carries an attribution.
Music tempo (70-90 bpm) is the script's reading of 'steady, flowing'; the user gave mood, instrument and 'no drums' only.
Arduino, Cremonese, Illy's Illetta and Cimbali are left out; no sentence in the script claims a count of inventors or that Gaggia worked alone.

beats.name: 리드 (Lead)
beats.job: State the result at once: the machine came first, the crema more than fifty years later.
beats.scene: What crema is and where it sits: espresso running into a cup and the tan foam forming on top.
beats.text: The order in time and the size of the gap (more than fifty years).

beats.name: 이름 (Name)
beats.job: Give the protagonist's name right after the lead.

beats.name: 시간순 전개 (In time order)
beats.job: Go back to 1884 and walk forward: Moriondo's steam patent, Bezzera's single cup, Pavoni's production, the 1906 fair where the name appears.
beats.scene: What the first machines looked like (the patent drawings themselves), which part made the single cup, the record's own words, how low 1.5 bar is on a dial.
beats.text: Who, in which year, for what purpose (economical and instant; fresh for a single cup), and the pressure figure.

beats.name: 심기 (Planting)
beats.job: Plant the repeated fact that the climax will break: for three more decades the needle never passes 2 bar, and the coffee is burned.
beats.scene: The needle trembling under the 2 mark while years pass; a cup of flat black coffee with nothing on top.
beats.text: How long it lasted, the ceiling (2 bar), the cause (steam) and the taste (bitter).

beats.name: 꺾임 (Turn)
beats.job: 1938: a bar owner replaces steam with a piston. War stops it; in 1947 the lever and spring arrive. The crema appears, and it is not sold as espresso.
beats.scene: How a piston pushes water through coffee; the nine-year gap on a timeline; a hand pulling a lever; the crema itself forming in a glass.
beats.text: The years, the patent, why nothing was built (war, no coffee imports), the cause of the foam (pressure, the coffee's oils), and the name it was sold under.

beats.name: 현재 (Now)
beats.job: Close the technical story: the 1961 pump holds the pressure steady; 9 bar is today's standard, six times the first machine.
beats.scene: The needle settling on 9 and the distance from 1.5 drawn as six steps.
beats.text: The year, what replaced the arm, the standard figure and the ratio.

beats.name: 결말 (Ending)
beats.job: Pause, show the first cup again, and set the patent's own word 'instant' against the fifty years.
beats.scene: The opening cup and its crema, unchanged.
beats.text: One fact: built to be instant, over fifty years to make this.

beats.name: 참고 자료 (Sources)
beats.job: Name the sources on one label card. The one disagreement that touches the lead (first crema in 1938 or 1947) is shown earlier, in the corner label of c03.
beats.scene: Small type on a dark frame.

cards.note: S2: higher pressure 'resulted in essential oils and colloids from the coffee creating a mousse or crema on top'. 'Oils' is a simplification of 'essential oils and colloids'.

visual.desc: The gauge, right third (meta.cast 'gauge'): the needle sweeps up and settles exactly on the heavy mark, which now receives its label '9'. In the left third, a line icon of a small pump with a switch that flips on.

cards.note: S2: the E61's electric pump meant espresso was produced 'under a relatively constant 9 bars'. S1: 'a motorized pump to provide the nine atmospheric bars'.

cards.label: Italian Espresso Institute

visual.desc: (앞 장면 계속) Same gauge: a faint second needle appears at 1.5, and an amber arc between 1.5 and 9 is divided into six equal steps.
visual.carries: The ratio made countable: six steps of 1.5 between the first machine and today's standard.
visual.motion: Camera: none / Subject: the arc fills step by step / Cut: cut to the cup

cards.note: Calculation: 9 ÷ 1.5 = 6 (9 bar: INEI standard, S9 and S2; 1.5 bar: Moriondo's boiler, S1). The Institute's parameter is 9 bar ± 1. Most recent support for 'today': S10 (2020), 'now the standard parameter for Italian espresso'. The Institute's current web page (iei.coffee, opened) describes the sensory profile only and does not list the pressure figure.

visual.desc: The opening clip again (c01): espresso streams into the small white cup on the dark counter and the tan foam builds. Cup in the lower third.
